storm.summary_layperson: No storm risk this evening — skies are clear, radar is empty, and there are no weather alerts, so the cove gets the same quiet, chilly night as every surrounding town.
storm.local_effect_blurb: No marine-layer buffer in play: air and Sound water are both about 54°F at 4 PM, and the air cools to roughly 43°F by 9 PM — about 11°F colder than the water — so the cove behaves like everywhere else tonight.
storm.detail_html:
Regional picture: high pressure is in control (about 1027 mb across every station from Westchester to Rhode Island) with a dry northwest flow and dewpoints in the mid 30s. The 4:44 PM radar scan shows no storm cells anywhere in range, there are no active National Weather Service alerts, and the forecast is simply sunny, turning clear and colder.

Ingredients for storms are absent. The atmosphere has zero available storm energy (CAPE of 0 J/kg) this evening and through the forecast hours. Winds aloft do change with height (about 27 kt of shear, easing to the low teens by 7 PM), but with no instability and no moisture there is nothing for that to organize.

Local effects: the cove's usual protection comes from warm air sitting over cooler Sound water, which starves incoming storms. That is not in play today — the Sound is 54°F and the air was about 54°F at 4 PM, so there is no gap at all. After the 4:34 PM sunset the air cools quickly while the water holds its temperature: about 50°F at 5 PM, 47°F at 6 PM, and near 43°F by 9 PM, leaving the air roughly 11°F colder than the water. There is no sea breeze either; every coastal station is blowing from the northwest, off the land.

Most likely outcome: a dry, clear, cooling evening in the cove, identical to surrounding towns. No rain, no thunder, and no storm arrival to time.

What would change the call: nothing on the horizon tonight. A storm threat would need a new moisture source and a front or disturbance moving in, and neither shows up in the observations, the radar, or the forecast for this window.

wind.regime_label: Moderate northwest gradient wind — no sea breeze, easing after dark

hourly.shift_note: light and patchy, holes near shore
light and patchy (carried forward from 9 PM)

wind.tactics_blurb: Northwest wind off the land means puffs and holes with big swings rather than a favored shore — best average pressure sits mid-cove, away from the lee of the western shoreline. Stay center, tack on the headers, and sail to the next puff; expect it to thin from about 7 kt to 5 kt as the evening cools.
wind.tactics_detail_html:
The call: a moderate gradient wind, with no sea breeze in play. The wind tonight is the large-scale northwest flow around high pressure, not anything thermal. A sea breeze needs the land at least 5°F warmer than the water; today the air–water temperature difference is essentially zero (air about 54°F, Sound 54°F) and turns negative after dark. None of the 19 coastal stations is blowing onshore, and the well-sited airport anemometers average 8 kt from the northwest.

What the cove has now: Riverside YC read NW to N at 9–10 kt just after 4 PM, with a 10-minute average of 7 kt and gusts near 11 kt. Bridgeport airport showed 11 gusting 16 kt an hour earlier. Because this is gradient wind it does not die with the sun — sunset was 4:34 PM and the whole window is after dark — but it does ease as the cooling ground layer stops mixing the stronger wind aloft down to the water. Expect about 7 kt at 5 PM, settling to roughly 5 kt from 8 PM on, with gusts shrinking from 11 kt toward 7–8 kt.

Why center: a northwest wind reaches the cove over land, trees and houses, so it arrives as puffs separated by holes, with 15–30° swings. Neither side of the course has a lasting edge; the steadiest average pressure is in the middle of the cove, clear of the immediate lee of the western shore. The cove station itself swung from 325° to 350° within three minutes this afternoon, which is exactly that character.

Shift character: oscillating, not persistent. The forecast direction holds at 324–326° through 7 PM, then eases about 10° left to roughly 313° from 8 PM. There is no front or boundary coming, so treat every shift as temporary: tack on headers and prioritise staying in pressure over picking a side.

Model versus observations: the HRRR model shows only 4–5 kt all evening, but it was reading 4 kt at 4 PM while the cove measured 7–10 kt, so the speeds here are scaled up toward the observations and then eased for the after-dark fade. Direction agrees well (model 322°, western-Sound stations about 310–320°). Because this is a gradient-wind day rather than a sea-breeze day, the sea-breeze direction correction does not apply.

On the water: 5–7 kt is light-air dinghy racing — raceable but finicky, with the gusts doing most of the work early and real holes near the shore later. It is also cold: about 50°F at 5 PM falling to the low 40s by 9 PM.

data_caveats: HRRR 20Z run had only posted through 9 PM at publish time — the 10 PM wind row is carried forward from 9 PM, not modeled

Wind speeds are adjusted upward from raw HRRR (which read 4 kt at 4 PM against 7–10 kt observed at Riverside YC); gusts are estimated from Riverside YC and Bridgeport gust-to-average ratios (no model gust field)
